The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $L$ be an observed baseline random element in a standard-Borel space [[def-standard-borel-space]],
$A$ a treatment random element [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] taking values in a nonempty countable set [[def-countable]] equipped with the discrete sigma-algebra (the full power set), following the treatment-version convention of [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]. Let $M$ be an observed mediator random element in a standard-Borel space [[def-standard-borel-space]], and let $Y$ be an observed real random variable [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. A **simple Markovian mediation SCM** is a
recursive structural causal model in the sense of
[[def-recursive-structural-causal-model-and-dag]] whose endogenous variables
are exactly $(L,A,M,Y)$ and whose equations have the form
$$L=f_L(U_L),\qquad A=f_A(L,U_A),\qquad M=f_M(A,L,U_M),\qquad Y=f_Y(A,M,L,U_Y).$$
The functions are jointly measurable in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], and the exogenous random elements
$U_L,U_A,U_M,U_Y$ are mutually independent [[def-independent-random-elements]], as required by the Markovian
condition in that SCM definition. The graph therefore has no latent common
cause outside $L$ and no additional post-treatment variable that causes both
$M$ and $Y$. This model is a special case of an NPSEM-IE (a nonparametric
structural equation model with independent errors); it is a substantive model
restriction, not a consequence of the observed distribution. It is a
single-unit model; if units interfere, the treatment version must include the
relevant joint assignment or exposure, as required by
[[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]].

The mediator and outcome responses are the recursive responses under the
interventions from [[def-controlled-and-natural-mediation-effects]]:
$$M(a)=f_M(a,L,U_M),\qquad Y(a,m)=f_Y(a,m,L,U_Y).$$
In particular, recursion gives $Y^a=Y(a,M(a))$. The model's absence of an
additional post-treatment common cause is part of the hypothesis; if such a
variable is present, this definition does not cover that causal system.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

derivations.claim: Let $g_A,g_M,g_Y$ be bounded measurable real functions and let $r$ be a bounded measurable function of $L$. By [F1], each response is a measurable function of $L$ and its own exogenous coordinate. The exogenous family is independent in the sense of [F2], so its joint law is the product law [F4]; Fubini integrates $U_A,U_M,U_Y$ separately, giving $E[r(L)g_A(A)g_M(M(a'))g_Y(Y(a,m))]=E[r(L)\alpha_A(L)\alpha_M(L)\alpha_Y(L)]$, where each $\alpha$ is the corresponding integral over one error law and is measurable by [F5]. The same event-testing calculation with two $g$'s set to $1$ identifies each $\alpha$ as the appropriate conditional-expectation version; testing against every $r$ gives the triple conditional-product identity.

Setting $g_A$, $g_Y$, and $g_M$, respectively, equal to $1$ in the triple conditional-product identity of step 1.1 gives $M(a')\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(a,m)\mid\sigma(L)$, $A\perp\!\!\!\perp M(a')\mid\sigma(L)$, and $A\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(a,m)\mid\sigma(L)$ by the bounded-function definition [F3]. These are exactly the three claims.

element $M$ in a standard-Borel space [[def-standard-borel-space]], and a real random variable $Y$ [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Let $M(a)$ be
the mediator response under $do(A=a)$ and let $Y(a,m)$ be the outcome response
under the joint intervention $do(A=a,M=m)$, with the intervention semantics of
[[def-recursive-structural-causal-model-and-dag]]. These are full-data random
variables; consistency alone does not identify their joint law from observed
data.

When the displayed differences are integrable [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], the **controlled direct
effect** at mediator setting $m$ is
$$\operatorname{CDE}_m(a,a')=E[Y(a,m)-Y(a',m)].$$
It requires that setting the mediator to $m$ be a meaningful intervention.
The **natural direct effect** and **natural indirect effect**, with $a'$ the
reference treatment level, are
$$\operatorname{NDE}(a,a')=E[Y(a,M(a'))-Y(a',M(a'))],$$
$$\operatorname{NIE}(a,a')=E[Y(a,M(a))-Y(a,M(a'))].$$
The first argument is the active outcome treatment level and the second is the
reference level that supplies the mediator response. When $a\ne a'$, these
targets involve nested counterfactuals from different intervention regimes.
They are defined on a full-data law whether or not they are identified by the
observed law. The total mean contrast is
$$\tau(a,a')=E[Y^a-Y^{a'}],$$
using the treatment-only potential outcomes of
[[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]. For $a=1,a'=0$, this agrees with
the ATE convention in [[def-causal-average-treatment-effects]].

The functions are jointly measurable in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], and the exogenous random elements
$U_L,U_A,U_M,U_Y$ are mutually independent [[def-independent-random-elements]], as required by the Markovian
condition in that SCM definition. The graph therefore has no latent common
cause outside $L$ and no additional post-treatment variable that causes both
$M$ and $Y$. This model is a special case of an NPSEM-IE (a nonparametric
structural equation model with independent errors); it is a substantive model
restriction, not a consequence of the observed distribution. It is a
single-unit model; if units interfere, the treatment version must include the
relevant joint assignment or exposure, as required by
[[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]].

The mediator and outcome responses are the recursive responses under the
interventions from [[def-controlled-and-natural-mediation-effects]]:
$$M(a)=f_M(a,L,U_M),\qquad Y(a,m)=f_Y(a,m,L,U_Y).$$
In particular, recursion gives $Y^a=Y(a,M(a))$. The model's absence of an
additional post-treatment common cause is part of the hypothesis; if such a
variable is present, this definition does not cover that causal system.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the conditional-expectation conventions. In a
simple Markovian mediation SCM, for every supplied treatment levels $a,a'$ and
mediator value $m$,
$$M(a')\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(a,m)\mid\sigma(L),$$
$$A\perp\!\!\!\perp M(a')\mid\sigma(L),\qquad A\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(a,m)\mid\sigma(L).$$
Thus independent structural errors supply the cross-world restriction needed
by the natural-effect formula, in addition to the single-world
treatment-outcome, treatment-mediator, and mediator-outcome independences.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Assume AC. Let $X$ and $Y$ take values in nonempty standard-Borel spaces $(E,\mathcal S)$ and $(T,\mathcal T)$ on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. Let $L$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, everywhere a probability kernel. There is a probability kernel $K:T\to E$ such that $L(\omega,\cdot)=K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ simultaneously outside a single null set. In fact, with the stated everywhere-kernel convention, the construction below gives this equality for every $\omega$. Consequently K is a conditional law of X given Y.

Assume AC for the countable determining-algebra supplier. If $K,L$ are regular conditional distributions of the same standard-Borel-valued random element $X$ given $\mathcal G$, there is one $N\in\mathcal G$ with $P(N)=0$ such that $K(\omega,\cdot)=L(\omega,\cdot)$ as measures for every $\omega\notin N$.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $K$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ given $\mathcal G$. For measurable $f:E\to[0,\infty]$, the measurable function $I_f(\omega)=\int f(x)K(\omega,dx)$ satisfies

$$\int_H I_f\,dP=\int_H f(X)\,dP\qquad(H\in\mathcal G).$$

This assertion is choice-free. Under AC, it says $I_f=E[f(X)\mid\mathcal G]$ as nonnegative almost-sure classes. If $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is measurable and $E|f(X)|<\infty$, put $D=\{I_{|f|}<\infty\}$. Then $D\in\mathcal G$, $P(D)=1$, and the signed integral on $D$, extended by zero off $D$, is a real integrable conditional-expectation version of $f(X)$. Its identification with the AC-based conditional-expectation class uses AC only for that class convention.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Fix a pair of treatment levels $a,a'$ in the simple Markovian mediation model
of [[def-simple-markovian-mediation-scm]]. The assumptions used for the
natural-effect formula are:

1. **Consistency and treatment versions.** The treatment versions and joint
   treatment/mediator interventions have the meanings fixed by
   [[def-controlled-and-natural-mediation-effects]]. The observed responses
   satisfy $M=M(A)$ and $Y=Y(A,M(A))$ by the structural recursion.

2. **No unmeasured treatment confounding.** Conditional on baseline $L$, the
   assignment error $U_A$ is independent of the mediator and outcome response
   errors. Equivalently in this model, for every supplied $b,c,m$,
   $A\perp\!\!\!\perp M(b)\mid\sigma(L)$ and
   $A\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(c,m)\mid\sigma(L)$.

3. **No unmeasured mediator–outcome confounding.** Conditional on $L$, the
   mediator and outcome response errors are independent. This excludes an
   unmeasured common cause of $M$ and $Y$ in the stated graph.

4. **No treatment-induced mediator–outcome confounder.** There is no
   post-treatment endogenous variable other than $M$ that is a common cause
   of $M$ and $Y$. If such a variable is present, the four-equation model
   above does not apply.

5. **Cross-world restriction.** For all supplied $b,c,m$,
   $M(b)\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(c,m)\mid\sigma(L)$. In particular this includes
   $M(a')\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(a,m)\mid\sigma(L)$ for the nested response in

under the joint intervention $do(A=a,M=m)$, with the intervention semantics of
[[def-recursive-structural-causal-model-and-dag]]. These are full-data random
variables; consistency alone does not identify their joint law from observed
data.

When the displayed differences are integrable [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], the **controlled direct
effect** at mediator setting $m$ is
$$\operatorname{CDE}_m(a,a')=E[Y(a,m)-Y(a',m)].$$
It requires that setting the mediator to $m$ be a meaningful intervention.
The **natural direct effect** and **natural indirect effect**, with $a'$ the
reference treatment level, are
$$\operatorname{NDE}(a,a')=E[Y(a,M(a'))-Y(a',M(a'))],$$
$$\operatorname{NIE}(a,a')=E[Y(a,M(a))-Y(a,M(a'))].$$
The first argument is the active outcome treatment level and the second is the
reference level that supplies the mediator response. When $a\ne a'$, these
targets involve nested counterfactuals from different intervention regimes.
They are defined on a full-data law whether or not they are identified by the
observed law. The total mean contrast is
$$\tau(a,a')=E[Y^a-Y^{a'}],$$
using the treatment-only potential outcomes of
[[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]. For $a=1,a'=0$, this agrees with
the ATE convention in [[def-causal-average-treatment-effects]].

Assume AC. Let $A$ be the countable-discrete treatment random element in
[[def-simple-markovian-mediation-scm]], let $L$ and $M$ be standard-Borel
random elements [[def-standard-borel-space]] [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], and let $Y$ be real-valued and integrable
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Suppose the
full-data law is a simple Markovian mediation SCM from
[[def-simple-markovian-mediation-scm]], with consistency, treatment positivity,
mediator positivity, and the integrability conditions of
[[def-natural-effect-identification-assumptions]]. Fix treatment levels
$a,a'$. Let $Q_b(l,dm)$ be a conditional law [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]] of $M$ given $(A,L)=(b,l)$, and
let $R((b,l,m),dy)$ be a conditional law [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]] of $Y$ given $(A,L,M)=(b,l,m)$.
Define the zero-filled conditional mean
$$\mu_b(l,m)=\begin{cases}\int y\,R((b,l,m),dy),&\int |y|R((b,l,m),dy)<\infty,\\0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
Then the nested mean
$$\theta(a,a')=E[Y(a,M(a'))]$$
is the following functional of the observed-data law:
$$\theta(a,a')=\int_{\mathcal L}\int_{\mathcal M}\mu_a(l,m)\,Q_{a'}(l,dm)\,P_L(dl),$$
where $P_L$ is the target-population law [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] of $L$. The support-domination
hypothesis $Q_{a'}(l,\cdot)\ll Q_a(l,\cdot)$ makes the integral independent
of the chosen conditional-mean version. Consequently,
$$\operatorname{NDE}(a,a')=\theta(a,a')-\theta(a',a'),\qquad \operatorname{NIE}(a,a')=\theta(a,a)-\theta(a,a')$$
are identified [[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]] in this model. The total mean contrast satisfies
$$\tau(a,a')=\operatorname{NDE}(a,a')+\operatorname{NIE}(a,a').$$
The formula is a population identification result; a regression coefficient
alone does not identify these effects.

Fix a pair of treatment levels $a,a'$ in the simple Markovian mediation model
of [[def-simple-markovian-mediation-scm]]. The assumptions used for the
natural-effect formula are:

1. **Consistency and treatment versions.** The treatment versions and joint
   treatment/mediator interventions have the meanings fixed by
   [[def-controlled-and-natural-mediation-effects]]. The observed responses
   satisfy $M=M(A)$ and $Y=Y(A,M(A))$ by the structural recursion.

2. **No unmeasured treatment confounding.** Conditional on baseline $L$, the
   assignment error $U_A$ is independent of the mediator and outcome response
   errors. Equivalently in this model, for every supplied $b,c,m$,
   $A\perp\!\!\!\perp M(b)\mid\sigma(L)$ and
   $A\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(c,m)\mid\sigma(L)$.

3. **No unmeasured mediator–outcome confounding.** Conditional on $L$, the
   mediator and outcome response errors are independent. This excludes an
   unmeasured common cause of $M$ and $Y$ in the stated graph.

4. **No treatment-induced mediator–outcome confounder.** There is no
   post-treatment endogenous variable other than $M$ that is a common cause
   of $M$ and $Y$. If such a variable is present, the four-equation model
   above does not apply.

5. **Cross-world restriction.** For all supplied $b,c,m$,
   $M(b)\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(c,m)\mid\sigma(L)$. In particular this includes
   $M(a')\perp\!\!\!\perp Y(a,m)\mid\sigma(L)$ for the nested response in
   the natural direct effect. The lemma
   [[lem-npsem-ie-implies-cross-world-independence-for-mediation]] proves
   this restriction for the simple NPSEM-IE model. The same-world instances
   $b=c$ express mediator–outcome exchangeability; the instances $b\ne c$
   are additional cross-world assumptions.

6. **Treatment positivity.** $P(A=b)>0$ and
   $P(A=b\mid\sigma(L))>0$ almost surely for each treatment level $b$ used
   in the contrast, in the target-support convention of
   [[def-positivity-for-discrete-treatment]].

7. **Mediator positivity.** Let $Q_b(l,\cdot)$ be a conditional law of $M$
   given $(A,L)=(b,l)$, in the sense of
   [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]. For the cross-treatment
   response $Y(a,M(a'))$, require
   $$Q_{a'}(l,\cdot)\ll Q_a(l,\cdot)$$
   for almost every $l$ under the law $P_L$ of $L$ from
   [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. This support-domination
   condition ensures that
   the conditional outcome law observed at treatment $a$ is defined at
   mediator values drawn under treatment $a'$. It is a measure-level
   condition; for a countable mediator it says every $m$ with
   $Q_{a'}(l,\{m\})>0$ also has $Q_a(l,\{m\})>0$.

8. **Integrability.** Every nested outcome $Y(b,M(c))$ used in the displayed
   effects is integrable [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]] under the target population law.

These are sufficient full-data assumptions for the theorem on this page, not
empirical facts certified by a regression fit. The NPSEM-IE independent-error
restriction supplies the cross-world condition. FFRCISTG means “Finest Fully
Randomized Causally Interpretable Structured Tree Graph”; in the single-world
convention described by Hernán–Robins, Chapter 23, its regime-specific laws do
not impose a joint independence between counterfactuals from incompatible
regimes. Thus FFRCISTG alone does not supply the cross-world condition above.
This item uses that source distinction only to name the missing assumption;
the explicit two-law counterexample is a separate B-page result. Standardizing
or fitting a regression does not by itself establish the assumptions above.

Hence the true nested means are $E[Y(1,M(0))]=E[U+W]=7/10$, $E[Y(1,M(1))]=E[U]+E[M(1)]=1$, and $E[Y(0,M(0))]=E[W]=1/5$. By [F1], the true natural effects are $\operatorname{NDE}(1,0)=1/2$ and $\operatorname{NIE}(1,0)=3/10$.
